gloss: A tool that writes with ink.
examples: Can I borrow a *pen*?
He signed the form with a blue *pen*.
All three *pens* in the drawer were dead.

gloss: A writing tool with a thin core of graphite inside wood.
examples: Do the first draft in *pencil* so you can erase it.
She sharpened her *pencil* down to a stub.
The kids left *pencils* all over the table.

gloss: A pen with a thick felt tip that writes in bold color.
examples: Somebody used a permanent *marker* on the whiteboard.
Label the box with a black *marker*.
Half these *markers* are dried out.
contrast: American; the British usually say felt-tip or marker pen.

gloss: A pen with bright see-through ink for marking text you want to find again.
examples: She went through the contract with a yellow *highlighter*.
My *highlighter* bled through the page.
I keep three *highlighters* in different colors.

gloss: A small piece of rubber for rubbing out pencil marks.
examples: The *eraser* on this pencil is worn down to nothing.
Can you hand me an *eraser*?
The teacher passes out *erasers* before the test.
contrast: American; the British say rubber. Americans give the s a hissed ss sound, not a z.

gloss: A stick of colored wax that children draw with.
examples: He drew the whole family in *crayon*.
There's a melted *crayon* in the back seat.
The restaurant hands out *crayons* with the kids' menu.

gloss: Soft white or colored stone pressed into sticks for writing on a board.
examples: The teacher wrote the date on the board in *chalk*.
Her hands were covered in *chalk* dust.
Grab a piece of *chalk* out of the box.
contrast: The l is silent: CHAWK. Uncountable — a piece of chalk, never a chalk.

gloss: The colored liquid that pens and printers write with.
examples: The printer is out of *ink* again.
Sign it in blue or black *ink*.
The rain smeared the *ink* on the envelope.

gloss: A book of blank or lined pages for writing in.
examples: I keep a *notebook* in my bag for lists.
She filled a whole *notebook* in one semester.
The *notebooks* are two for a dollar this week.

gloss: A flat paper cover that a letter goes inside for mailing.
examples: Put a stamp on the *envelope* and drop it in the mail.
The check came in a plain white *envelope*.
I bought a box of *envelopes* at the drugstore.
contrast: Two American pronunciations are common: EN-vuh-lohp and AHN-vuh-lohp.

gloss: A small printed square you stick on mail to pay for delivery.
examples: This letter needs another *stamp*.
He's collected *stamps* since he was a kid.
A book of *stamps* went up in price again.

gloss: A folded cover of stiff paper, or a place on a computer, that holds documents together.
examples: Everything for the meeting is in the blue *folder*.
I saved the file to the wrong *folder*.
She keeps separate *folders* for each client.

gloss: A stiff cover with rings inside that holds punched pages.
examples: My notes are all in a three-ring *binder*.
He dropped the *binder* and the pages went everywhere.
Bring your *binders* to class on Monday.

gloss: A device that fastens sheets of paper together with small metal staples.
examples: Does anybody have a *stapler*?
The *stapler* is jammed again.
There are two *staplers* in the supply closet.

gloss: A bent piece of wire that holds a few sheets of paper together.
examples: Just put a *paperclip* on it for now.
She straightened out a *paperclip* to reset the router.
There's a bowl of *paperclips* by the printer.

gloss: A flat strip marked with inches or centimeters for measuring and drawing straight lines.
examples: Use a *ruler* so the line comes out straight.
The *ruler* in my desk is only six inches.
The teacher handed out *rulers* for the drawing.

gloss: The set of keys you type on.
examples: I spilled coffee on my *keyboard*.
She uses a Russian *keyboard* at home.
Both *keyboards* stopped working after the update.

gloss: A smooth white board that you write on with erasable markers.
examples: He sketched the whole plan out on the *whiteboard*.
Somebody erased the *whiteboard* before I copied it down.
There are *whiteboards* in every conference room.

gloss: Paper, envelopes, pens, and other supplies for writing.
examples: The *stationery* is in the cabinet by the copier.
She writes thank-you notes on nice *stationery*.
We spend a fortune on office *stationery*.
contrast: Stationery with an e is paper and pens; stationary with an a means not moving. They sound identical.

gloss: The marks such as commas and periods that break writing into readable pieces.
examples: Your *punctuation* is all over the place in this paragraph.
The text came through with no *punctuation* at all.
We spent a whole week on *punctuation* rules.

gloss: The dot that ends a sentence.
examples: You forgot the *period* at the end of that line.
Put a *period* there, not a comma.
He writes in short sentences with a lot of *periods*.
contrast: American; the British call this mark a full stop.

gloss: The mark that separates parts of a sentence.
examples: You need a *comma* before the word and.
She took out half the *commas* in my draft.
One *comma* changes the whole meaning of that sentence.

gloss: The mark of two stacked dots that introduces a list or an explanation.
examples: Put a *colon* after the heading and then list the items.
The title has a *colon* in the middle of it.
He uses *colons* everywhere in his emails.

gloss: The mark that joins two closely related sentences.
examples: A *semicolon* would work better than a period there.
Nobody in the office knows how to use a *semicolon*.
Her writing is full of *semicolons*.

gloss: The raised mark used in contractions and to show possession.
examples: It's spelled with an *apostrophe* between the t and the s.
You left the *apostrophe* out of don't.
Ordinary plurals don't take *apostrophes*.
contrast: Four syllables with the stress in the middle: uh-PAHS-truh-fee.

gloss: The short line that joins two words into one.
examples: Is well-known written with a *hyphen*?
Her last name has a *hyphen* in it.
American style drops the *hyphens* in a lot of these words.
contrast: A hyphen (-) joins words; the longer dash (—) sets a phrase off from the rest.

gloss: The star-shaped mark used to flag a note or an exception.
examples: The cheap fares all have an *asterisk* next to them.
Put an *asterisk* by the ones you're not sure about.
The fine print is marked with *asterisks*.
contrast: Ends in -risk: AS-tuh-risk. AS-tuh-riks is a very common slip.

gloss: One of the square marks used to enclose something added to a quotation.
examples: The editor's note is in *brackets*.
Anything in *brackets* was added later.
Close the *bracket* at the end of the line.
contrast: In American usage ( ) are parentheses and [ ] are brackets; the British call ( ) brackets.

gloss: The forward-leaning line used between alternatives or in web addresses.
examples: Write and/or with a *slash* between them.
There's an extra *slash* in that link.
The date is written with *slashes*.
contrast: The line leaning forward is a slash; the one leaning the other way is a backslash.

gloss: The low line used in file names and usernames in place of a space.
examples: My username has an *underscore* in it.
Use an *underscore* instead of a space in the file name.
The address has two *underscores*.

gloss: The symbol that stands for the word and.
examples: The company name is written with an *ampersand*.
Use an *ampersand* only if the logo does.
Old shop signs are full of *ampersands*.

gloss: The mark that shows a shout, surprise, or strong feeling.
examples: One *exclamation point* is plenty.
She ends every text with an *exclamation point*.
The email had three *exclamation points* in the subject line.
contrast: American; the British say exclamation mark.

gloss: The mark that ends a question.
examples: You left off the *question mark*.
That sentence needs a *question mark*, not a period.
His notes are covered in *question marks*.

gloss: One of the pair of marks that enclose someone's exact words.
examples: Put his exact words in *quotation marks*.
She made *quotation marks* in the air with her fingers.
The closing *quotation mark* is missing.
contrast: Americans use double marks where the British often use single ones.

gloss: A large form of a letter, used to begin a sentence or a name.
examples: Start the name with a *capital*.
The whole sign was in *capitals*.
You typed my last name without a *capital*.
contrast: The letter is a capital; the state government building is a capitol. Same sound, different spelling.

gloss: A word that names a person, place, thing, or idea.
examples: Table is a *noun* and eat is a verb.
Circle every *noun* in the paragraph.
German capitalizes all its *nouns*.

gloss: A word that names an action or a state.
examples: Every sentence needs a *verb*.
The *verb* has to agree with the subject.
English has a lot of irregular *verbs*.

gloss: A word that describes a noun.
examples: Blue is an *adjective* in that sentence.
Cut half the *adjectives* out of your first draft.
In English the *adjective* usually comes before the noun.

gloss: A word that tells how, when, or where something happens.
examples: Quickly is an *adverb*.
Most *adverbs* in English end in -ly.
She dropped the *adverb* and the line got stronger.

gloss: A short word such as he, it, or they that stands in for a noun.
examples: Use a *pronoun* so you don't repeat the name.
It isn't clear what *pronoun* she is referring to.
English has fewer *pronouns* than Russian does.

gloss: A small word such as in, on, or of that shows how words relate.
examples: Is it interested in or interested about? It's the *preposition* that trips people up.
Don't worry about ending a sentence with a *preposition*.
The *prepositions* are the hardest part of English for me.

gloss: A word such as and, but, or because that joins parts of a sentence.
examples: And is the most common *conjunction* in English.
Start the second half with a *conjunction*.
He strings whole paragraphs together with *conjunctions*.

gloss: A word such as wow or ouch that expresses sudden feeling.
examples: Ouch is an *interjection*.
The line is just an *interjection* and a comma.
Comic books are full of *interjections*.

gloss: The form of a verb that shows when something happens.
examples: Keep the whole story in the past *tense*.
You switched *tense* in the middle of the paragraph.
English *tenses* take a while to sort out.
contrast: In fast speech tense sounds almost exactly like tents; only context tells them apart.

gloss: The word in a sentence that receives the action of the verb.
examples: In I read the book, book is the *object*.
The verb takes a direct *object*.
Underline the subjects and circle the *objects*.
contrast: The noun is AHB-jikt with the stress up front; the verb meaning to protest is uhb-JEKT.

gloss: The part of a sentence that tells what the subject does or is.
examples: Split the sentence into subject and *predicate*.
The *predicate* starts at the verb.
We diagrammed *predicates* for two weeks straight.
contrast: The noun ends in -kuht; the verb meaning to base something on ends in -kayt.

gloss: A small group of words that work together but do not make a full sentence.
examples: In a nutshell is a common *phrase*.
Cut that *phrase* and the sentence reads better.
She keeps a list of useful *phrases* for meetings.

gloss: A word or group of words that describes or limits another word.
examples: Walking down the street, the house looked empty — that's a dangling *modifier*.
Move the *modifier* next to the word it describes.
The sentence is buried under three *modifiers*.

gloss: The verb form ending in -ing or -ed that works like an adjective or builds a tense.
examples: Broken is the past *participle* of break.
Use the present *participle* after the verb to be.
The irregular *participles* are the ones you have to memorize.

gloss: The basic form of a verb, usually written with to in front of it.
examples: To go is the *infinitive*.
Nobody really cares about splitting an *infinitive* anymore.
Dictionaries list verbs as *infinitives*.

gloss: The -ing form of a verb used as a noun.
examples: Swimming in that sentence is a *gerund*.
After enjoy you need a *gerund*, not an infinitive.
Some verbs take *gerunds* and some take infinitives.

gloss: The set of forms a verb takes for different persons and tenses.
examples: Write out the full *conjugation* of the verb.
The *conjugation* is irregular in the past.
Spanish has three *conjugations*.

gloss: The class a noun belongs to in some languages, such as masculine or feminine.
examples: Russian nouns have *gender*, and English ones don't.
You have to learn the *gender* along with the word.
German has three *genders*.

gloss: The sound a person makes when speaking or singing.
examples: I didn't recognize her *voice* on the phone.
Keep your *voice* down in the library.
I could hear *voices* in the next room.

gloss: The form of a word used for more than one.
examples: The *plural* of child is children.
Add an s to make the *plural*.
English has a handful of irregular *plurals*.

gloss: The form of a word used for just one.
examples: The *singular* of these is this.
The verb has to match the *singular* subject.
News looks plural but it takes a *singular* verb.

gloss: A piece added to the front of a word that changes its meaning.
examples: Un- is the *prefix* in unhappy.
Add the *prefix* re- to mean again.
Half these words share the same two *prefixes*.

gloss: A piece added to the end of a word that changes its meaning or its part of speech.
examples: The *suffix* -ness turns an adjective into a noun.
Drop the final e before you add the *suffix*.
Learn a few common *suffixes* and you can guess a lot of words.

gloss: The letters at the end of a word that show its grammatical form.
examples: The verb takes an -s *ending* in the third person.
Russian nouns change their *endings* depending on the case.
He keeps dropping the past-tense *ending*.

gloss: The form of an adjective or adverb that compares two things.
examples: Bigger is the *comparative* of big.
Use the *comparative* when you're comparing two people.
Long adjectives make their *comparatives* with more.

gloss: The form of an adjective or adverb that marks the most or the least.
examples: Best is the *superlative* of good.
Put the in front of a *superlative*.
Ads are full of *superlatives*.
contrast: The stress falls on the second syllable: soo-PUR-luh-tiv, not SOO-pur-lay-tiv.

gloss: The way words are actually used by the people who speak a language.
examples: That spelling is fine in American *usage*.
The dictionary has a note on *usage* at the bottom.
*Usage* changes faster than the rule books do.
contrast: The s hisses here: YOO-sij. The verb use has a z sound: YOOZ.

gloss: A statement of how something is supposed to be done.
examples: The *rule* is i before e except after c.
That *rule* has more exceptions than examples.
Grammar *rules* are easier to state than to follow.

gloss: A single unit of language, written with spaces on either side.
examples: I don't know that *word* — let me look it up.
Say it in your own *words*.
The essay has to be under five hundred *words*.

gloss: A single beat of sound in a word.
examples: Banana has three *syllables*.
The stress falls on the second *syllable*.
Say it slowly, one *syllable* at a time.

gloss: A speech sound made with the mouth open, or the letter that spells it.
examples: A, e, i, o, and u are the *vowels*.
The *vowel* in cat is short.
He writes text messages with no *vowels* at all.

gloss: A speech sound made by blocking the air, or the letter that spells it.
examples: Strength ends in three *consonants* in a row.
The first *consonant* is silent in knife.
Russian has some *consonants* that English doesn't.

gloss: The set of letters a language is written with, in their fixed order.
examples: The English *alphabet* has twenty-six letters.
File them in *alphabet* order.
Russian and Greek use different *alphabets*.

gloss: The smallest unit of sound that can change the meaning of a word.
examples: Pat and bat differ by one *phoneme*.
English has about forty-four *phonemes*.
That *phoneme* doesn't exist in her first language.

gloss: The way someone's speech sounds because of where they come from.
examples: She still has a slight *accent*.
He can do a pretty good Southern *accent*.
There are dozens of *accents* just in this state.

gloss: The rise and fall of the voice across a sentence.
examples: Questions in English have rising *intonation*.
Your grammar is fine, but the *intonation* sounds off.
You can hear the sarcasm in the *intonation*.

gloss: The large form of letters, such as A and B.
examples: The whole headline is in *uppercase*.
Type the code in *uppercase*.
Passwords have to mix *uppercase* and lowercase.

gloss: The small form of letters, such as a and b.
examples: Her name is styled in all *lowercase*.
The password field is *lowercase* only.
Switch that heading to *lowercase*.

gloss: A word written the wrong way.
examples: There's a *misspelling* in the very first line.
That *misspelling* made it onto the printed sign.
The résumé had three *misspellings*.
contrast: Two s's in the middle: mis- plus spelling.

gloss: A shortened form of a word or phrase.
examples: St. is the *abbreviation* for street.
Spell it out the first time, then use the *abbreviation*.
The form is full of *abbreviations* nobody explains.

gloss: A word made from the first letters of a phrase.
examples: NASA is an *acronym*.
Every department invents its own *acronym*.
The manual is nothing but *acronyms*.

gloss: The first letter of a name, used in place of the whole name.
examples: Just put your *initials* at the bottom of each page.
The towels are monogrammed with her *initials*.
He signs everything with a single *initial*.
contrast: Usually used in the plural: sign your initials, not sign your initial.

gloss: A word that means nearly the same as another word.
examples: Big and large are *synonyms*.
Find a *synonym* so you're not repeating yourself.
The thesaurus gives twelve *synonyms* for happy.

gloss: A word that means the opposite of another word.
examples: Hot is the *antonym* of cold.
Match each word with its *antonym*.
The worksheet asks for three *antonyms*.

gloss: A word spelled or said the same as another but meaning something different.
examples: Bat the animal and bat the stick are *homonyms*.
That pun turns on a *homonym*.
English is loaded with *homonyms*.

gloss: A word that sounds like another word but is spelled differently.
examples: There and their are *homophones*.
Spell-check won't catch a *homophone*.
Half my mistakes are *homophones*.

gloss: What a word, sign, or sentence stands for.
examples: What's the *meaning* of that word?
The word has a second *meaning* in medicine.
One comma can change the *meaning* completely.

gloss: A set phrase whose meaning is not the sum of its words.
examples: Kick the bucket is an *idiom*.
You can't translate an *idiom* word for word.
American English is full of baseball *idioms*.

gloss: Very informal words used mostly in speech among a particular group.
examples: Don't use *slang* in a cover letter.
Teenage *slang* changes every couple of years.
Half of what he says is *slang* I've never heard.
contrast: Uncountable: a piece of slang or a slang word, never a slang or two slangs.

gloss: The special vocabulary of a trade or profession, hard for outsiders to follow.
examples: The report is buried in legal *jargon*.
Try to explain it without the *jargon*.
Every industry has its own *jargon*.
contrast: Uncountable: a piece of jargon, never a jargon or jargons.

gloss: A form of a language spoken in one region or by one group.
examples: She grew up speaking a mountain *dialect*.
The word only exists in that *dialect*.
The country has dozens of *dialects*.

gloss: The set of special words used in a particular field.
examples: The medical *terminology* threw me.
We need to agree on the *terminology* first.
Legal *terminology* hasn't changed much in centuries.

gloss: The history of where a word came from.
examples: The *etymology* of salary goes back to salt.
The dictionary gives the *etymology* in brackets.
He can rattle off *etymologies* for hours.

gloss: Someone who studies how language works.
examples: She's a *linguist* who works on child speech.
A *linguist* would tell you that's a normal sound change.
The team hired two *linguists*.
contrast: In American usage a linguist is a language scientist; someone who simply speaks many languages is a polyglot.

gloss: The word or words a person or thing is called by.
examples: What's the *name* of that street?
I forgot her *name* the second she said it.
Put your *names* at the top of the page.

gloss: An informal name used instead of someone's real name.
examples: Everyone calls him by his *nickname*.
Where did that *nickname* come from?
The team gives out *nicknames* to the rookies.

gloss: The family name that comes after a person's given name.
examples: Smith is the most common *surname* in the country.
She kept her *surname* after the wedding.
Both *surnames* are hyphenated on the form.
contrast: Americans usually say last name in speech and keep surname for forms and paperwork.

gloss: The ability to speak or write a language easily and smoothly.
examples: The job asks for *fluency* in Spanish.
Six months abroad did wonders for her *fluency*.
Accuracy comes before *fluency* in the early stages.

gloss: The ability to read and write.
examples: *Literacy* rates have climbed steadily.
The library runs an adult *literacy* program.
The grant is for early childhood *literacy*.

gloss: One of the parts a piece of writing is divided into.
examples: The rules are in *section* four.
That whole *section* can be cut.
The report has six *sections* and an appendix.

gloss: The short title printed above a section of text.
examples: Put a *heading* over each part.
The *heading* is in bold.
Just skim the *headings* to find it.

gloss: A short piece taken out of a longer text.
examples: Read the *passage* and answer the questions.
She quoted a *passage* from the letter.
The test has four reading *passages*.

gloss: A short account that gives only the main points.
examples: Write a one-paragraph *summary*.
Skip to the *summary* at the end.
The *summaries* are due Friday.

gloss: A short summary printed at the head of a paper or article.
examples: I only read the *abstract*.
The *abstract* has to fit in two hundred words.
You can search the *abstracts* without paying.
contrast: The noun stresses the first syllable, AB-strakt; the adjective meaning not concrete is ab-STRAKT.

gloss: A set of items written one after another.
examples: Add milk to the *list*.
Her name isn't on the *list*.
I make *lists* for everything.

gloss: An account of connected events, told as a story.
examples: The book is a first-person *narrative*.
The two witnesses gave completely different *narratives*.
Break up the *narrative* with some dialogue.

gloss: A short well-known phrase that states a piece of common sense.
examples: There's an old *saying* about that.
As the *saying* goes, better late than never.
My grandmother had *sayings* for every occasion.

gloss: A short traditional sentence that gives advice.
examples: A stitch in time saves nine is an old *proverb*.
There's a Russian *proverb* that says the same thing.
The book collects *proverbs* from around the world.

gloss: A puzzling question asked as a game.
examples: He told me a *riddle* I couldn't solve.
The answer to the *riddle* is a shadow.
Kids love telling *riddles*.

gloss: A word that ends in the same sound as another, or a poem built on such words.
examples: Orange famously has no *rhyme*.
The song is just a *rhyme* repeated four times.
She learned the alphabet through *rhymes*.
contrast: The h is silent and comes after the r: r-h-y-m-e, pronounced RYM.

gloss: A phrase that calls one thing another to make a point.
examples: Time is money is a *metaphor*.
That *metaphor* falls apart if you push it.
His speech was full of sports *metaphors*.

gloss: A comparison that uses like or as.
examples: Cold as ice is a *simile*.
A *simile* says like; a metaphor doesn't.
The poem opens with two *similes*.
contrast: Three syllables, SIM-uh-lee. It has nothing to do with the word smile.

gloss: A joke that plays on two meanings of a word.
examples: That's a terrible *pun*.
The headline is a *pun* on the movie title.
The menu is nothing but bad *puns*.

gloss: Something said to make people laugh.
examples: He told the same *joke* twice.
I didn't get the *joke*.
Her *jokes* land better in person.

gloss: The particular words chosen to say something.
examples: The *wording* of the contract is deliberately vague.
Change the *wording* so it doesn't sound rude.
Legal *wording* takes some getting used to.

gloss: Something said briefly about someone or something.
examples: That was an unkind *remark*.
She made a *remark* about the weather and moved on.
His closing *remarks* ran twenty minutes.

gloss: The line that leans back, used in file paths on Windows.
examples: The path uses a *backslash* between folders.
Type a *backslash*, not a regular slash.
The code is full of *backslashes*.
contrast: The backslash leans back; the one in web addresses leans forward and is just a slash.

gloss: The small wavy mark written above a letter or used to mean about.
examples: Spanish puts a *tilde* over the n.
A *tilde* in front of a number means roughly.
Both file names end in *tildes*.
contrast: Commonly TIL-duh in American speech, though you'll also hear TIL-dee.

gloss: Slanted type used for emphasis and for titles.
examples: Book titles go in *italics*.
The *italics* are mine, not the author's.
Put the foreign word in *italics*.
contrast: Always has the -s ending and takes a plural verb: the italics are mine.

gloss: Thick, dark type used to make words stand out.
examples: The key terms are in *boldface*.
Set the heading in *boldface*.
Too much *boldface* and nothing stands out.

gloss: The blank space at the start of a line of text.
examples: Each paragraph starts with a half-inch *indent*.
The *indent* is inconsistent on page three.
The code uses two-space *indents*.
contrast: The noun stresses the first syllable, IN-dent; the verb is in-DENT.

gloss: The way text is laid out on a page — fonts, spacing, margins, and the rest.
examples: The *formatting* fell apart when I opened it on my phone.
Strip the *formatting* before you paste it in.
Follow the *formatting* in the sample.

gloss: A written symbol that stands for a number.
examples: The clock face uses Roman *numerals*.
Write the year as a *numeral*, not a word.
Arabic *numerals* are used almost everywhere now.
contrast: American NOO-mur-uhl, without the y sound the British put after the n.

gloss: An empty space left in a text for someone to write in.
examples: Fill in the *blank* with the right verb.
Leave the last *blank* empty for now.
The worksheet has twenty *blanks*.

gloss: The way a particular person forms letters by hand.
examples: I can't read his *handwriting*.
Her *handwriting* is neater than the printout.
The note was in my mother's *handwriting*.
contrast: Uncountable: her handwriting is neat, never her handwritings.

gloss: Handwriting in which the letters are joined together.
examples: They barely teach *cursive* in school anymore.
Sign it in *cursive*, not block letters.
My *cursive* is a mess.
contrast: American; the British call it joined-up writing.

gloss: Careless or unreadable marks made with a pen or pencil.
examples: There's a *scribble* in the margin I can't make out.
The signature is just a *scribble*.
The wall was covered in kids' *scribbles*.

gloss: A change made to fix a mistake.
examples: The teacher wrote a *correction* over every error.
The paper printed a *correction* the next day.
Make these *corrections* and send it back.

gloss: A changed version of a piece of writing, or the work of changing it.
examples: The second *revision* is much tighter.
It went through four *revisions* before anyone liked it.
The whole chapter needs a *revision*.
contrast: In American English revision means rewriting; in Britain it also means studying for an exam.

gloss: Reading a text carefully to catch mistakes before it is published.
examples: The draft still needs *proofreading*.
She does *proofreading* on the side.
An hour of *proofreading* caught nine errors.

gloss: The act of writing with a keyboard.
examples: His *typing* is faster than my handwriting.
I did all my own *typing* for the thesis.
The class starts with ten minutes of *typing*.

gloss: A paper copy of something from a computer.
examples: Bring a *printout* of the schedule.
The *printout* came out crooked.
There are *printouts* on every chair.

gloss: A small pad of paper for jotting things down.
examples: He carries a *notepad* in his shirt pocket.
I wrote the number on a *notepad* by the phone.
There are *notepads* in every hotel room.

gloss: A pen that writes with a tiny rolling ball at the tip.
examples: A cheap *ballpoint* works better on that paper.
The *ballpoint* leaked all over my pocket.
There's a cup of *ballpoints* on the counter.

gloss: A small device that puts a point back on a pencil.
examples: The *sharpener* is mounted by the door.
Does anybody have a *sharpener*?
Both *sharpeners* are full of shavings.

gloss: A small piece of paper with glue on the back.
examples: She got a gold star *sticker* on her homework.
There's a price *sticker* still on the bottom.
His laptop is covered in *stickers*.

gloss: An older machine that prints letters onto paper as you press its keys.
examples: He still writes first drafts on a *typewriter*.
The old *typewriter* is missing the letter e.
The shop repairs *typewriters*.

gloss: One item in a list marked with a small dot.
examples: Turn that paragraph into a *bullet point*.
Keep each *bullet point* to one line.
The slide has too many *bullet points*.

gloss: The # symbol.
examples: Enter your code, then press the *pound sign*.
The *pound sign* is above the three on my keyboard.
The message ended with two *pound signs*.
contrast: Americans call # the pound sign or the number sign; the British call it hash.

gloss: The @ symbol, used in email addresses and usernames.
examples: My address is my last name, *at sign*, the company name.
The *at sign* is over the two.
Usernames start with *at signs* on most apps.

gloss: A small mark written over a letter to show stress or a change of sound.
examples: Café is spelled with an *accent mark*.
English almost never uses an *accent mark*.
French has several different *accent marks*.

gloss: A small stiff card used for notes.
examples: Write one fact per *index card*.
He gave the speech off an *index card*.
I studied from a stack of *index cards*.

gloss: A yellow lined writing pad with a glued top edge.
examples: He took notes on a *legal pad* the whole meeting.
There's a *legal pad* in the top drawer.
The supply closet is out of *legal pads*.
contrast: A standard American office item; the yellow color is what people picture.

gloss: A pen that draws liquid ink from a reservoir inside it.
examples: He signs contracts with a *fountain pen*.
The *fountain pen* skips on cheap paper.
She collects vintage *fountain pens*.

gloss: A computer check that flags misspelled words.
examples: Run a *spell-check* before you send it.
The *spell-check* didn't catch their instead of there.
Two *spell-checks* later there were still typos.

gloss: The name your parents gave you, which comes before the family name.
examples: Just use my *first name*.
The form asks for your *first name* and middle initial.
There are three people here with the same *first name*.

gloss: The family name that comes at the end of a person's full name.
examples: What's your *last name*, so I can look you up?
They have the same *last name* but they're not related.
Alphabetize the list by *last name*.

gloss: A language made of hand shapes and movements instead of sounds.
examples: She's been learning *sign language* since middle school.
There was an interpreter doing *sign language* beside the stage.
Different countries have different *sign languages*.

gloss: The messages a person sends through posture, gesture, and expression.
examples: His *body language* said he wanted to leave.
Watch her *body language* during the interview.
A lot of meaning comes across in *body language*.
contrast: Uncountable: read his body language, never his body languages.

gloss: Someone who grew up speaking a particular language.
examples: A *native speaker* would never phrase it that way.
The class is taught by a *native speaker*.
Half the *native speakers* I asked disagreed.

gloss: The number of words in a piece of writing.
examples: What's the *word count* on the essay?
I'm three hundred over the *word count*.
Magazines have strict *word counts*.
